label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
liked_the_characters: Deck, the fussy one who sends slides back, and the mortified designer are the ones I would hire; the others are a little thin and the owning-up is a touch too neat.
page_one_why: The slide-compromise opening is personal and the factory is defined in one clear sentence, but it is about a speaker and a talk, and I run a publication, so I had to translate it myself.
what_the_team_did: A handful of agents with named roles were set up in an hour, ran on their own clock for a day while checking and arguing with each other, were stopped once by the editor, and were then rebuilt for the next job.
why_it_matters_to_me: It is a working model of a small newsroom of agents with me as the editor who signs and the one person who can lift the brake.
tomorrow: Open an empty project with one agent, write a one-page rules file (what it may change, when it stops and asks me) and a brief for a single daily story, with sources listed under every claim.

won_over.quote: a second reading, not a second identity.
won_over.why: An honest limit on agent review is what I need to hear before I trust a checker, and it is what earns my trust.

won_over.quote: Anyone in the factory could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: That is the editor's control stated plainly, and it is more than a rubber stamp.

won_over.quote: My reviewer said a file was not mine to change. I showed it was.
won_over.why: A dispute resolved on evidence is the newsroom habit I want.

won_over.quote: Add a second agent only when the first is busy.
won_over.why: A concrete, sensible rule for growing the team slowly.

stuck.quote: the editor's chair is empty from five in the morning to two in the afternoon.
stuck.why: Nine hours with no signature sits oddly with my need for an editor who signs; I wanted to know what was allowed to ship unseen.

stuck.quote: Nobody was watching, and they argued, sent work back, owned their mistakes and kept the books.
stuck.why: A strong claim, and agents performing remorse may just be fluent; I wanted evidence of outcomes, not manners.
Scenes are invented dialogue on a record, which jars when I am exacting about sources; the reader needs to be told on the page, not in a note.

stuck.quote: The checks worked, and they also missed.
stuck.why: It does not say what was missed, or how often, so I cannot judge how far to trust the checks.

would_share: Another independent publisher or newsletter writer who is already experimenting with agents; not my readers, as it is about how to build and not about what I publish.

your_questions.a: Yes: a team of agents assembled in an hour around one objective, run for a day, taken apart afterwards, with the human as the one who can stop and restart it.

your_questions.q: Would you start tomorrow, and with which role?
your_questions.a: Yes, with one agent in the conductor's role, setting the rules and the brake, then a researcher whose every claim must carry a source.

your_questions.q: Where would you not trust it?
your_questions.a: Where a reviewer shares the same session and reach as the agent it checks, and in the nine hours without the editor, where I want to see which pieces went out unsigned. Also the invented dialogue, until it is clearly marked.

page_one.why: Warm and clear on the factory, but its frame is a conference talk, not a publication.

clarity.why: The arc is easy to follow and the page 10 steps are concrete; the jargon is glossed late or not at all.

for_someone_like_me.why: The newsroom example appears only as a one-line aside, but the researcher, reviewer and signing editor map directly onto my work.

would_start.why: Five small steps, no private data, a free account to begin; I would want the sourcing rule in the first page of rules.

notes: No text in the sample tried to direct me. I ignored the record codes and Band lines as instructed. A newsroom example with sources shown would lift page 10 for me.
